newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. urges North Korea not to heighten tensions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges North Korea not to heighten tensions.

text.p: The United States urged communist North Korea to avoid all provocative actions as a diplomatic standoff continued over a high Pyongyang official holed up at South Korea's embassy in Beijing.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson was speaking after the shooting of a North Korean defector outside his home near the South Korean capital Seoul, an attack the South has blamed on communist agents.

Richardson said the United States was closely watching developments after Saturday night's attack which left 32-year-old defector Li Il-nam critically ill in hospital with a bullet still lodged in his skull.
Seoul officials said the assassination attempt appeared to be a North Korean warning to Seoul and to potential asylum-seekers. The government hiked security for public figures and installations.
"This is an incident that is serious," Richardson said on ABC Television's "This Week" programme.

"We urge North Korea to live up to the agreement that they made on the submarine incident, when they apologised, and part of that agreement with South Korea was, number one, that they not engage in provocative actions."
He was referring to North Korea's apology for sending a spy submarine to a South Korean beach last September and landing 26 armed commandos who were then captured.

Meanwhile the man at the centre of the Beijing drama -- Hwang Jang-yop, 73-year-old top adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il -- was spending his sixth day in the South Korean mission, behind a tight Chinese security cordon.
Hwang, a member of the secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, arrived there by taxi on Wednesday.

South Korea says Hwang is seeking asylum in the South, while a furious North Korea insists he was kidnapped. Hwang was ranked 24th in the Stalinist state's hierarchy, and would be the most senior Pyongyang official to seek asylum in the South.
Hwang's betrayal has caused a massive loss of face for a North Korean government already reeling from severe food shortages and economic disasters.
It has cast a heavy pall over North Korea's planned celebrations to mark strongman Kim Jong-il's 55th birthday on Sunday.

Lavish birthday celebrations for the Dear Leader, as Kim is known in his Stalinist homeland, had been intended to smooth his formal accession to supreme power after the death of his father, Great Leader Kim Il-sung, three years ago.

In the event, the party appeared subdued, scaled down to little more than fireworks and a gymnastics display by 10,000 children. Scheduled live broadcast coverage by the official media was abruptly cancelled without explanation.
China played for time over Hwang's fate, agonising over how to usher him out of Beijing without offending its old socialist ally or its new capitalist friend.
It has urged calm on the Korean peninsula, where two of the world's largest armies face each other, while it investigates Hwang's real intentions.

Chinese security was taking no chances of trouble at the South Korean mission, on a normally quiet, tree-lined street in the Chinese capital's eastern diplomatic quarter. Armed police set up a fortress-like defence wall, laying anti-tyre spikes across approaches and bringing in a huge water cannon truck.
Pyongyang diplomats were keeping constant watch outside the security cordon.
"We are determined to prevent them from taking him to the South," said the official, who declined to give his name.
